claims.text: The proposed target material is a homogenized, single-phase FCC CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with a uniform grain structure.
The target high-entropy alloy has moderate-to-low stacking-fault energy.
Loading single-phase FCC HEAs at strain rates of 10^3–10^5 s−1 rapidly nucleates and moves partial dislocations.
High-strain-rate loading produces stacking faults, partial-dislocation pile-ups, and mechanical twins in the HEA.
Partial dislocations and twins form transient stacking-fault and twin networks during dynamic loading.
Twin boundaries and associated fault structures impede dislocation motion and thereby strengthen the alloy.
Intersecting twin-boundary/matrix interfaces provide additional pathways for dislocation glide and cross-slip.
The coexistence of dislocation barriers and additional deformation pathways can jointly produce strength and ductility.
This strength–ductility mechanism operates specifically under dynamic loading at 10^3–10^5 s−1.
Relative to a simpler FCC control, the HEA will exhibit a higher work-hardening rate.
Relative to a simpler FCC control, the HEA will exhibit a higher peak flow stress.
Relative to a simpler FCC control, the HEA will preserve ductility or delay fracture under dynamic loading.
The HEA will preserve or delay necking during the proposed high-rate compression test.
The enhanced mechanical response will coincide with greater partial-dislocation, stacking-fault, and twinning activity at advanced strain than in the control.
The mechanism should hold for single-phase FCC HEAs with moderate-to-low stacking-fault energy near ambient temperature.
The mechanism may cease to dominate when phase transformations or other deformation modes become active.
The relative contributions of slip and twinning depend on composition, grain size, and temperature.
A lack of increased partial-dislocation or twinning activity in the HEA during high-rate loading would falsify the proposed twin–dislocation synergy.

contradictions.description: The experiment is specified as dynamic compression, but delayed necking is listed as an expected observation; conventional necking is a tensile-instability measure and is not directly applicable to a compression-only SHPB test.
